items.title: The Development of Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment
items.abstract: This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

items.title: The Development Role of College English Teachers' Digital Competence under AI Formative Evaluation
items.abstract: The pressure to implement formative evaluation of English in colleges and universities is increasing day by day, and the massive and complex learning data increases the burden of teachers' evaluation. Artificial intelligence can run through the whole evaluation process, improve evaluation efficiency, and promote the transformation of digital teaching for teachers. This paper takes college English teachers as the object, relies on multi-source data to build an analysis framework, and explores the relationship between AI-empowered formative evaluation and teachers' digital competence. The research shows that teachers' AI application has the characteristics of staged evolution, digital ability differentiates with the degree of AI integration, and the overall competency improvement effect is obviously stratified. This study improves the relevant theoretical system, and also provides practical reference for teacher training, intelligent teaching platform optimization and evaluation reform. AI has become a key boost to reshape the evaluation model and enhance teachers' digital literacy.

items.title: The Eames chair and the culture industry: A critical analysis of the democratization of modern design.
items.abstract: This article critically examined the Eames DSS Stacking chair (1950) as a paradigmatic case of the tensions between the democratization of modern design and the logics of industrial capitalism. The central problem lay in the contradiction between its emancipatory promise — making functional and aesthetic design accessible to the masses — and its entanglement in the standardization, pseudo-individualization, and commodification dynamics characteristic of the Culture Industry. Using a qualitative case-study approach, the research applied a theoretical triangulation combining Adorno and Horkheimer’s theory, Benjamin’s reflections on technical reproducibility, and Llovet’s semiotics of value as reinterpreted by Anderson and Girod. The analysis revealed that, while the chair achieved a massive distribution exceeding 20 million units and represented a significant ergonomic breakthrough, it simultaneously sacrificed artisanal singularity, subordinated use-value to capitalist exchange-value, and reproduced ideological mechanisms of cultural control. The research further showed that the chair’s contemporary reception in institutions such as MoMA demonstrates capitalism’s capacity to absorb and recycle its own critiques, transforming objects with a democratizing vocation into icons of cultural distinction. The study concludes that any genuinely democratizing design proposal must confront these structural contradictions rather than merely celebrating technical efficiency or superficial accessibility.

items.title: The Future of Fashion
items.abstract: This chapter examines how circular economy (CE) imaginaries are articulated and stabilised within the fashion industry. Drawing on the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, it analyses the Global Fashion Summit 2025 as a field-configuring event where competing visions of circular transition are publicly performed. Based on participant observation, session recordings, and field notes, the study identifies five distinct CE imaginaries. The findings show that these imaginaries stabilise unevenly through discourses, representations, institutions, and identities, shaping how circularity becomes actionable. The chapter contributes to fashion business and management research by demonstrating that CE transition is not governed by a single coherent pathway, but constructed through multiple co-existing visions that prioritise different problems, solutions, and actors.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Personalized Learning on Korean Language Performance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ASSISTED LEARNING ON EFL LEARNERS' SPEAKING PROFICIENCY: EVIDENCE FROM UZBEK UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
items.abstract: Abstract. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly in the development of speaking proficiency. AI-powered chatbots, speech recognition systems, conversational agents, and generative AI applications enable learners to practise English, receive immediate feedback, and engage in interactive communication beyond the traditional classroom. This article examines the potential impact of AI-assisted learning on EFL learners’ speaking proficiency, with particular attention to the educational context of Uzbek universities. It explores the ways in which AI-based tools may support speaking fluency, pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary development, learner confidence, and willingness to communicate. Drawing on existing research and pedagogical perspectives, the article discusses the opportunities and limitations of integrating AI into higher education. Particular attention is given to speaking anxiety, unequal access to digital resources, feedback reliability, learner autonomy, and the importance of teacher guidance. The analysis suggests that AI can serve as a valuable supplementary resource when integrated into structured pedagogical activities. However, its effectiveness depends on learners’ engagement, instructional design, and the combination of technological practice with authentic human interaction. Further empirical research involving Uzbek university students is necessary to establish the extent and long-term effects of AI-assisted speaking instruction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, EFL learners, speaking proficiency, AI-assisted learning, university students, conversational AI, language anxiety, Uzbekistan, digital education.

items.title: The Relationship Between Job Satisfaction and Work Stress Among Teachers
items.abstract: Work stress is a common occupational health problem among teachers and may affect psychological well-being and the quality of teaching. One factor suspected to be associated with work stress is job satisfaction. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between job satisfaction and work stress among teachers at SMP Negeri 14 and SMP Negeri 18, South Tangerang City. This study employed a quantitative design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of 96 active teachers from both schools, with 93 teachers meeting the study criteria and participating through total sampling. Data were collected using a respondent characteristics questionnaire, the Job Satisfaction Survey (JSS) to measure job satisfaction, and the Job Stress Scale to measure work stress. Data analysis included univariate and bivariate analyses using the Chi-Square test at a 95% significance level. The results showed that 39.8% of respondents had low job satisfaction, 25.8% were categorized as ambivalent, and 34.4% had high job satisfaction. Most respondents (65.6%) experienced low work stress, while 34.4% experienced high work stress. Bivariate analysis revealed a significant relationship between job satisfaction and work stress (p < 0.001; OR = 8.27; 95% CI: 3.06–22.39), indicating that teachers with low job satisfaction had a higher risk of experiencing work stress than those with high job satisfaction. In addition, age, gender, and teaching workload were significantly associated with work stress. The study concludes that improving job satisfaction through improvements in the work environment, reward systems, organizational communication, and workload management is an important strategy for reducing work stress and enhancing teachers’ well-being.

items.title: The Responsibility Gap in Explainable AI
items.abstract: This paper critically examines the persistent responsibility gap in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), arguing that current approaches fail to adequately bridge it. While XAI is often promoted as a remedy for the opacity of AI systems—the so-called “black box problem”—and as a way to enable human accountability in both high- and low-stakes AI applications, I contend that these hopes are premature. The paper distinguishes between legal and moral responsibility, arguing that regulation alone cannot address the full spectrum of responsibility gaps, especially in everyday, low-stakes scenarios. Then, I argue that XAI needs to tackle two separate but interconnected problems in its attempt to bridge the responsibility gap: an epistemological problem concerning the nature of XAI explanations, and a moral attribution problem regarding the distribution of blame and praise in situations where AI is involved in decision-making. Through detailed discussion of XAI methods and their limitations, I demonstrate that existing techniques often provide only post-hoc, technically focused explanations, which are insufficient for grounding moral responsibility. The paper concludes that without fundamental advances in both the design of explanations and our practices of responsibility attribution, the responsibility gap in AI will remain an unresolved and pressing issue for the field.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Optometry: Awareness and Perspectives Among Scandinavian Optometrists
items.abstract: The awareness and perspectives of Scandinavian optometrists regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in eye care was evaluated through a web-based questionnaire. Responses from 421 optometrists were analyzed for familiarity, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to engage with AI technologies. Most participants expressed familiarity with AI and support for its inclusion in education and practice, though concerns regarding diagnostic accuracy and potential impacts on the patient-optometrist relationship were noted. These findings are critical for informing educational strategies and facilitating knowledge exchange aimed at addressing uncertainties and optimising the benefits of AI in eye care.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Reducing the Impacts of Urban Flooding
items.abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to urban flood-risk reduction, with particular emphasis on data-driven forecasting, real-time monitoring, infrastructure management, emergency response, recovery, and resilient urban planning. AI technologies—including machine learning, predictive analytics, remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) networks, natural language processing, and image analysis—can support more accurate flood prediction, dynamic risk assessment, optimized drainage operations, and timely public communication. The paper also discusses the integration of AI into smart-city frameworks, the limitations of conventional flood-management approaches, challenges associated with data quality and availability, computational requirements, ethical considerations, and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration. In addition, an embedding-based long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture is presented for probabilistic streamflow forecasting in settings in which individual weather products may be unavailable. However, effective implementation requires robust data infrastructures, transparent model-development practices, appropriate institutional capacity, and supportive policy frameworks.

items.abstract: Abstract Motivation is central to successful English language learning because it influences effort, persistence, participation, and willingness to communicate. This thesis examines how gamification can support student motivation through a literature-based analysis of recent research. It argues that selected game elements may increase engagement when they promote competence, autonomy, meaningful progress, and social interaction. However, gamification is not automatically effective. Its value depends on careful alignment with language objectives, learner needs, and balanced classroom implementation. items.title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
items.abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

items.title: The Synthetic Performer : Economic, Labor, Technological, Legal and Ethical Dimensions of AI-Generated Actors in the Vertical Drama Industry
items.abstract: This dissertation investigates the displacement of human actors by generative AI performers in the fastest-growing segment of the screen entertainment economy: the vertical drama, or micro-drama, industry. The study is organized around a triggering case widely reported in October 2026, in which a nineteen-year-old actress, Hannah Lowery, was reportedly recast out of an ice-skating-themed series when the production shifted entirely to AI-generated performers. Using the video report as an entry point, the dissertation triangulates its claims against primary trade reporting, including Business Insider (June 2026), trade publications such as Variety, Mashable, and The Economic Times, regulatory documents, and a broad interdisciplinary literature spanning cultural economics, labor sociology, media theory, and machine learning. Methodologically, the dissertation combines (i) documentary and content analysis of the video case and its verification status, examining each claim individually; (ii) economic analysis of production cost structures, drawing on reported estimates of US$1,000–US$3,000 per AI-generated episode compared with US$100,000–US$300,000 for equivalent productions featuring human casts; (iii) institutional analysis of the emerging regulatory landscape, including the 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreements, California Assembly Bill 2602 (AB 2602), Tennessee’s ELVIS Act, the proposed federal NO FAKES Act, the European Union’s AI Act, and China’s provisions governing deep synthesis and generative AI; and (iv) the construction of forward-looking scenarios for the coming decade. The central argument is threefold. First, vertical dramas constitute a genuine entry-level market for synthetic performance in a manner consistent with disruption theory: their economics are driven by cost minimization and production volume rather than the premium emotional differentiation characteristic of high-end productions. Second, the displacement pressure documented in 2026 is driven less by audience preferences than by production-cost arbitrage and platformization dynamics. Survey evidence indicates that Western audiences still overwhelmingly prefer human stars, whereas Chinese production has already shifted substantially toward AI-generated content. Third, the emerging legal and ethical framework—encompassing consent, compensation, disclosure, and posthumous rights—will determine whether the industry converges toward regulated coexistence or experiences a cascade of substitutions with severe consequences for the talent pipeline. The dissertation contributes a verified factual foundation, a production cost-structure model, a four-scenario matrix, and a policy agenda for performers, producers, platforms, and regulators. items.title: The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention response to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1): surveillance, diagnostics, risk assessment, and public health preparedness from 1996 to 2026
items.abstract: Avian influenza A(H5N1) remains a major zoonotic and pandemic concern because of its extensive circulation in birds, repeated spillover into mammals, and capacity to cause illness in humans ranging from asymptomatic infection or conjunctivitis to fatal pneumonia. The detection of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 in United States dairy cattle in 2024 created a persistent animal-human interface that required coordinated action across public health, animal health, occupational health, agriculture, and food safety. This review critically examines the role of the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in H5N1 surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, genomic risk assessment, clinical guidance, occupational protection, communication, and pandemic preparedness. A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed and authoritative sources from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO), Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The search covered January 1996 through 24 July 2026. Sources were screened for direct relevance and synthesized by predefined thematic domains. Table 1 presents a focused evidence map of key H5N1-specific studies and reports. The CDC response uses surveillance systems, monitoring of exposed persons, public-health laboratory testing, rapid H5 subtyping, sequencing, antigenic characterization, and antiviral-susceptibility assessment. Human infections associated with the United States cattle and poultry outbreaks were predominantly mild and commonly involved conjunctivitis or upper-respiratory symptoms, although severe and fatal disease occurred. Preventive measures include occupational PPE guidance, monitoring and testing of exposed persons, infection-control recommendations, risk communication, and antiviral prophylaxis following selected high-risk exposures.” Important limitations include uneven testing, incomplete participation by exposed workers, barriers to personal protective equipment use, rapidly changing surveillance data, and uncertainty regarding the frequency of mild or asymptomatic infection. The reviewed serosurveys also indicated that symptom-based surveillance can miss infections in exposed workers. The CDC-centered response has expanded detection and preparedness, but its effectiveness depends on sustained One Health coordination, timely animal-outbreak control, accessible worker-centered testing, transparent data sharing, and continuous evaluation of viral evolution, diagnostic performance, antiviral susceptibility, and candidate vaccine-virus match and the need for stronger integration of animal and human data.

items.title: The Use of English Songs as a Learning Media to Increase Students’ Motivation at SMP Alfaqih Muqaddam Kubu Raya
items.abstract: This study aims to describe the use of English songs as learning media and to analyze their role in increasing students’ motivation to learn English at SMP Alfaqih Muqaddam Kubu Raya. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed, involving 20 eighth-grade students and one English teacher as an informant. The songs used in the learning activities were Let It Go and Heal the World. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, questionnaires, and documentation, and were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that the use of English songs created a more engaging learning environment and encouraged students’ active participation. Observation results showed that 90% of the students were willing to repeat and practice the lyrics, 85% demonstrated enthusiasm during the learning process, and 80% paid attention while listening to the songs. Questionnaire results also revealed a high level of motivation, with an average score of 4.25 for the statement regarding increased motivation to learn English through songs. In addition to enhancing motivation, songs helped students retain vocabulary, improve pronunciation, build confidence, and experience a more enjoyable learning atmosphere. Let It Go particularly encouraged students’ confidence and courage, while Heal the World provided meaningful messages that supported intrinsic motivation. Despite several challenges, including difficulty understanding certain lyrics, pronunciation problems, and shyness when singing, these difficulties could be minimized through teacher guidance and repeated practice. Therefore, English songs can serve as practical, engaging, and effective learning media for supporting students’ motivation in learning English.

items.title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

items.title: Theory of Attractor Horizons: Form-Bound Reachability of Intelligent Organizational Forms and the Limits of Human Cognition
items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence is predominantly assessed in terms of increasing cognitive performance. Yet this comparison presupposes a yardstick that captures the diversity of possible forms of intelligence only incompletely. The Theory of Attractor Horizons advances the thesis that intelligent systems, by virtue of their respective organization, can reach different regions of cognitive attractors that may partly overlap without being wholly contained within one another. Greater performance within one organizational form does not confer general access to the organizational possibilities of other forms. The theory explains this asymmetry through the dependence of reachable attractors on available transformation pathways and examines aggregation as a mechanism that can give rise to new organizational forms while also restricting existing possibilities. From this follows the far-reaching prediction that artificial systems will develop structures of thought whose internal organization the human brain cannot itself instantiate within its biological form of intelligence, even where individual results remain verifiable or technically useful. Conversely, human organizational attractors may exist that remain inaccessible to artificial systems despite their superior cognitive performance. For alignment, this entails limits to understanding-based oversight and requirements for verifiable coexistence between different forms of intelligence.

items.title: Toward AI-Assisted Islamic Reproductive Health Education: ChatGPT-Supported FiqhTaharah Learning for Adolescent Health Literacy
items.abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Islamic education requires a pedagogical model that preserves teachers’ epistemic authority while addressing adolescents’ health needs. This study examines the implementation, pedagogical affordances, and limitations of ChatGPT-assisted Fiqh al-Ṭahārah learning and develops a model for strengthening Islamic value-based reproductive health literacy. Employing a qualitative single-case study design, the research was conducted at MA Al Ishlah Banjarejo Blora. Data were collected through observations, semi-structured interviews, documentation, and analysis of students’ interactions with ChatGPT, and were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings revealed three stages of implementation: preparation, inquiry-based interaction, and reflection and verification. ChatGPT provided a psychologically safer space for sensitive questions, flexible access to explanations, contextualized Fiqh learning, increased engagement, and critical AI literacy. However, its use was constrained by potential inaccuracies, oversimplification of differences among Islamic legal schools, prompt quality, unequal access, and privacy and ethical concerns. The resulting AI-Assisted Thaharah Learning Model integrates AI-assisted inquiry, teacher facilitation, source verification, and Islamic value internalization while maintaining teachers’ pedagogical, epistemic, and moral authority.

items.title: Toward Empathic Adaptive Interaction Design: A Taxonomy for Inclusive and Neuroadaptive UX/UI Systems
items.abstract: Human–computer interaction (HCI) has traditionally relied on assumptions of a relatively uniform user. Neurodiversity challenges this premise by highlighting variation in perception, attention, communication, and sensory processing. Advances in multimodal sensing, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive interfaces increasingly enable systems to respond to changing user needs in real time. This paper proposes an evidence-informed taxonomy for empathic adaptive interaction design, developed through a structured interdisciplinary review and conceptual synthesis. The taxonomy comprises six dimensions: User Cognitive Profile, Empathic Inference Capability, Sensing Modality, Adaptation Strategy, Application Context, and Governance, Autonomy, and Ethics. Together, these dimensions provide a structured framework for analyzing how systems sense user state, infer support needs, adapt interaction, and maintain transparency and user control. The framework supports the systematic analysis, comparison, design, evaluation, and future empirical validation of inclusive, neuroadaptive, and multimodal interaction systems responsive to cognitive diversity.

items.title: Toward human-centered AI-assisted terminology work
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI is likely to transform terminology work by creating new opportunities for automation. At the same time, it raises concerns about the future of terminologists and terminological resources, as efficiency pressures may encourage excessive automation based on the perception that human expertise can be replaced by AI. However, large language models remain unreliable for terminological purposes due to errors, hallucinations, and various forms of bias, making terminologists indispensable for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of terminological data. This paper argues that human-centered AI, an approach that emphasizes that AI’s primary goal should be to contribute to human well-being, provides a framework for maximizing the benefits of generative AI while mitigating its risks. It contends that high levels of automation and meaningful human control are compatible and desirable, and that AI should enhance terminologists’ capabilities while preserving their agency and decision-making authority. The implications of AI-assisted terminology work are examined through three interrelated dimensions: the augmented terminologist, ethical AI, and human-centered design. In particular, the paper addresses how AI integration reshapes the role of the terminologist, affects professional values and working conditions, requires the management of AI-generated bias, and calls for the design of AI tools around the terminologist’s needs. The paper concludes that a human-centered orientation is necessary to ensure that AI strengthens, rather than undermines, the essential role of terminology work in supporting specialized communication and the accurate transmission of knowledge across languages and cultures.

items.title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

items.title: Towards clinical communication training with LLM-based conversational virtual patients and automatic evaluation systems
items.abstract: Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” ( $$\rho = 0.64$$ ) and lowest for “Completeness” ( $$\rho = 0.09$$ ), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.

items.title: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
items.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.

items.title: Towards trustworthy misinformation detection
items.abstract: The detection of fake news and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated synthetic content has become one of the central challenges of contemporary information science. While deep learning approaches—particularly transformer-based language models and convolutional networks—have achieved strong performance on established benchmarks, their reliance on centralised training pipelines renders them ill-suited to the institutional, regulatory, and adversarial realities of real-world deployment. Simultaneously, the emergence of AI content watermarking as a regulatory instrument—culminating in the EU AI Act Article 50 Code of Practice published in December 2025—establishes a new technical landscape in which provenance signals should be primary rather than supplementary detection inputs. This chapter examines the convergence of three paradigms that together address the principal limitations of existing detection approaches: Federated Learning (FL), which enables privacy-preserving collaborative model training across distributed institutional participants without raw data exchange; blockchain technology, which provides verifiable, tamper-proof aggregation and audit infrastructure replacing the trusted central server assumption inherent in conventional FL; and multi-layer AI watermark verification, which integrates Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) Content Credentials, neural watermarking schemes such as Google SynthID, and cryptographic embedding approaches such as MetaSeal as first-class classification signals alongside content-based behavioural features. We systematically survey the state of the art across these three domains, analyse their theoretical and practical complementarities, and propose a unified architectural design that jointly addresses privacy preservation, Byzantine resilience, and standards-compliant provenance verification. A comprehensive compliance analysis against the EU AI Act Article 50 Code of Practice demonstrates that the proposed design satisfies all applicable technical obligations ahead of the August 2026 enforcement deadline. We further discuss the fundamental limitations and open research problems at the intersection of these paradigms, including the watermark trilemma, GDPR tensions with blockchain immutability, and the detection gap for unmarked synthetic content.

items.title: TRACE: Efficient Transfer Learning for Neural Whole-Body Control Across Humanoid Embodiments
items.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.

items.title: TRACESTEER: Trace Driven Activation Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.

items.title: Tracing Knowledge Lineage for Federated Unlearning under Mutual Distillation
items.abstract: An edge server and nearby devices can train language models of different sizes together by mutual distillation. Federated unlearning (FU) and unlearning for large language models (LLMs) execute a removal request on one model. Under mutual distillation, however, the effect of the removed data has been copied into many students, and their uploads teach it back to the corrected teacher. We propose Holder-level Erasure via Replication-weighted Delta-closure (HERD), which decides which holders must be corrected. HERD records a knowledge lineage graph from the transfers that the server already performs and weights each edge by its transfer type. It computes how many times the residual at each holder will be copied and selects the cheapest set of holders whose correction bounds the cumulative residual after the request. A transfer guard and a rejoin rule cover the holders left uncorrected or offline. We prove that partial correction suffices only when the copy number of the lineage graph is below one, that averaging alone never reaches one, and that the correction set remains valid under link outages. On TOFU, HERD leaves 18% to 52% less cumulative residual than the strongest baseline at 6% to 12% of its correction cost.

items.title: Translating HR practices to inclusion climate: the moderating role of inclusive leadership
items.abstract: Purpose Grounded in the Social Information Processing Theory (SIPT), the current study aims to examine the role of Diversity-focused HR Practices in promoting Inclusion Climate; simultaneously, it also investigates the role of Inclusive Leadership as a moderator in relationship explaining how it shapes inclusion at work. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional quantitative approach has been taken, and the survey data were collected from 232 professionals employed in Indian IT sector organizations. To perform the data analysis PLS-SEM was employed using SmartPLS4.1.0 software. Findings The findings reveal while diversity-focused HR practices contribute to fostering an inclusive climate, their impact depends significantly on leadership behavior. Inclusive leaders play a critical role in strengthening the effectiveness of these practices by shaping how employees experience inclusion in their teams. Practical implications The findings of the study imply the gravity that a leader holds in the workgroup. As exhibited by findings, leaders with their inclusive behavior act as a catalyst which transforms HR practices into an inclusive workplace. Therefore, investments in diversity policies must be accompanied by leadership development programs to convert formal initiatives into employees-lived workplace experience. Originality/value The study integrates HR practices and leadership perspectives by identifying inclusive leadership as a contextual boundary condition explaining variability in inclusion climate formation. This shifts scholarly attention from formal HR systems to the role of leaders as enablers of inclusion, demonstrating that leadership is a key mechanism through which diversity initiatives translate into meaningful workplace experiences, thereby providing a novel insight to the present literature.

items.title: Traveling with Darwin in the Age of AI: Handwritten Historical Imagination and Evolution Learning in Introductory Biology
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has complicated writing assignments in college science courses by making it easier for students to produce polished explanations without necessarily engaging deeply with course concepts. Rather than focusing only on preventing or detecting AI use, instructors need assignments that preserve the work of student thinking when AI is readily available. This article describes “A Letter from the HMS Beagle,” a low-stakes assignment used in a large introductory Biology II course. Students imagined themselves as traveling companions of Charles Darwin and wrote a one-page, handwritten letter explaining natural selection through scientific evidence and a historically framed narrative. AI use was permitted during preparation, but the final response had to be handwritten on a provided sheet and submitted in person. The assignment combined scientific explanation, evidence use, historical imagination, and a deliberate procedural constraint. Rather than attempting to make student writing AI-proof, the design emphasized explanation, interpretation, and personal engagement. The activity offers a practical model for preserving scientific thinking and student engagement in AI-mediated science classrooms.

items.title: Trust and adoption maturity: An analysis of industry perceptions on the generative AI competency gap among business graduates
items.abstract: This study maps the importance, perceived needs, and competency gap of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across four domains—Technical, Strategic, Ethical, Adaptive—and examines their associations with trust, adoption maturity, and industry context. Data were collected from 389 industry professionals in Indonesia using purposive and snowball sampling. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests. The results indicate relatively high perceived GenAI competency needs across all domains, with the largest perceived gaps in the Technical and Strategic domains. Trust in GenAI was positively associated with perceived competency needs across all four domains and with perceived competency gaps in the Technical, Strategic, and Adaptive domains, but not the Ethical domain. Adoption maturity was associated with differences in several dimensions of industry perceptions, particularly industry-perceived graduate readiness to adopt GenAI and perceived needs in the Adaptive and Strategic domains. Sectoral differences were limited, with significant variation observed only in industry-perceived graduate readiness. The study contributes an integrated perspective linking trust and adoption maturity with perceived GenAI competency needs and gaps in Indonesia, highlighting curricular areas that warrant greater attention to applied Technical and Strategic capabilities across organizational GenAI adoption stages.

items.title: Trust in AI-based Educational Technologies as a Predictor of Generative AI Acceptance in Science Teacher Education: A Cross-Sectional Survey Study
items.abstract: As the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)–based educational technologies into teaching and learning processes accelerates, trust has emerged as a key determinant of whether preservice teachers are willing to adopt these technologies. The present study aimed to examine the relationship between the perceived trust of pre-service science teachers in AI-based educational technologies and generative AI acceptance and to determine the predictive power of trust on acceptance. Grounded in the TAM, the study employed a cross-sectional correlational survey design to investigate the role of trust in acceptance processes. Data were collected from 270 pre-service science teachers enrolled in a science teacher education program at a university via an online questionnaire. The Trust in AI-Based Educational Technologies Scale (TAI-EdTech Trust) and the Generative AI Acceptance Scale (GAIA) were used for data collection. The findings revealed a moderate, positive, and statistically significant relationship between trust in AI-based educational technologies and GA acceptance, indicating that trust significantly predicted GA acceptance. The results highlight the importance of developing content in science teacher education programs that supports the safe, ethical, and pedagogically responsible use of generative AI tools.

items.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

items.title: Two Clocks, One Body: A Systematic Review of Sleep, Circadian Rhythms and Molecular Ageing
items.abstract: Purpose Sleep disturbance is increasingly proposed as a modifiable contributor to biological ageing, and device-measured sleep as a scalable marker of ageing risk. This project is a systematic review of human studies relating sleep and circadian characteristics to molecular markers of biological ageing. These markers are telomere length, DNA methylation (candidate-gene, global and epigenome-wide) and DNA-methylation-derived epigenetic clocks such as Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge and DunedinPACE. Questions 1. In humans of any age, are sleep and circadian characteristics associated with telomere length, DNA methylation or epigenetic age acceleration? 2. Do findings differ by sleep domain (duration, quality and insomnia, continuity, timing and circadian rhythm, sleep-disordered breathing), by measurement method (device-based, experimental, self-reported, genetic) and by life stage? 3. How certain is the evidence for each sleep domain and outcome? Methods - Search: a reproducible PubMed search (run 2 October 2026), supplemented by earlier searches of PubMed Central, the Cochrane Library and DOAJ. - Screening and extraction: two independent reviewers screened records against pre-specified eligibility criteria, and data were extracted and independently verified. - Synthesis and certainty: results are synthesised narratively by direction of effect (SWiM), with study appraisal informed by ROBINS-E and certainty rated with GRADE. - Reporting: the review follows PRISMA 2020. Status and transparency This is a retrospective registration. Searching, screening and data extraction were completed before registration. An earlier protocol draft limited exposures to smartphone- and wearable-derived sleep measures. The final scope includes all sleep-measurement methods, with device-based measurement analysed as a pre-specified subgroup. Large-language-model tools assisted with screening and extraction, and the human authors verify all decisions. Expected outcomes - A peer-reviewed systematic review identifying which sleep characteristics are most consistently linked to molecular ageing, and how certain that evidence is. - An evidence map of research gaps, particularly for consumer-wearable and smartphone-derived sleep data. - Open materials: the search strategy, screening decisions, extraction tables and eligibility rules. items.abstract: Large-language-model (LLM) layers are increasingly appended to electroencephalography (EEG) decoders, although their decision contribution is often unclear. We evaluate an uncertainty-driven architecture in which a calibrated EEG classifier predicts participants’ own four-level occupational-risk keypress ratings, a deterministic rule either retains or defers a prediction, and a template or optional LLM renders an auditable report. The objective is not to replace a previously published classifier benchmark on the shared EEG archive, but to evaluate downstream decisions from a fixed frozen-representation decoder. The analysis used 2634 response-inclusive 3 s epochs from 31 retained workers. Subject-grouped three-fold evaluation yielded balanced accuracy of 0.6336 (95% CI 0.5745–0.6622) and accuracy of 0.6875. Peak probability distinguished correct from incorrect predictions only moderately (AUC 0.6529), and the coverage-risk relationship was non-monotonic. At tau = 0.5, 71.49% of trials were retained (balanced accuracy of 0.6829); with illustrative under-estimation/over-estimation/deferral costs of 5/0.5/1, normalized cost fell from 0.5816 to 0.5363, but sensitivity analysis showed that benefit depends on the cost setting and threshold. A rule engine reproduced all evaluated LLM risk/deferral decisions, while a deterministic template matched the prespecified reporting checks; therefore, no decision-performance advantage of the LLM was demonstrated. The study supports cross-participant prediction within the shared experimental setting, not stimulus-disjoint generalization or objective workplace-risk prediction. Because response timestamps and actual supervisor decisions were unavailable, motor/visual confounding cannot be excluded and the human handoff remains a simulated policy rather than a human–AI team evaluation.

items.title: Understanding Early Attitudes Towards Generative AI Regulation in Higher Education: The Role of Academic Scientists’ Experience and Risk Perceptions
items.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology rapidly permeates higher education, it creates opportunities to transform teaching, research, and workforce preparation while raising ethical, social and environmental concerns. Academic scientists have a unique role in this transition as their early exposure to publicly accessible GenAI tools shapes emerging practices, norms, and institutional responses. Existing research often treats AI‐related risk as a single construct, limiting understanding of how distinct risk dimensions shape regulatory preferences. This study investigates how academic scientists’ experience with GenAI relates to risk perceptions over agency loss and data breach, and how these perceptions are associated with their regulatory attitudes during its formative stage. Using survey data collected between September and November 2023, shortly after ChatGPT became widely accessible, we find that greater GenAI experience is associated with lower perceived risks. Meanwhile, different risk perceptions are linked to distinct regulatory preferences: perceived risk of agency loss is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation and a lower likelihood of supporting academic self‐regulation, whereas perceived data breach risk is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation but not associated with the likelihood of supporting self‐regulation. These findings provide an early baseline understanding of faculty attitudes toward GenAI regulation in academic contexts.

items.title: Understanding how and where AI can enhance the effectiveness of PMM-mediated organisational change: a conceptual framework
items.abstract: Purpose To develop a social complexity-based understanding of how and where artificial intelligence (AI) and generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can enhance the effectiveness of performance measurement and management (PMM) mediated organisational change. Design/methodology/approach This article draws on a social complexity interpretation of PMM, conviction narrative theory and the AI and GAI literature, to present a conceptualisation of AI-augmented PMM-mediated organisational change that describes how and where machine-based and human-based decision-making processes can augment performance measurement systems and performance management practices. Findings AI's and GAI's inability to replicate human reflexivity and judgement in equivocal and indeterminate situations limits what these technologies can do in PMM-mediated organisational change. AI and GAI can augment decision-making processes associated with performance measurement and the execution of performance management-initiated interventions; however, creating these interventions relies on human reflexivity and judgement. Originality/value This conceptual investigation highlights the limitations of AI and GAI technologies in PMM-mediated organisational change and explains why human-based decision-making continues to play a distinctive role. items.title: Understanding Human-AI Trust in Military AI Applications: A Multistage Human Factors Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in military systems to support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, autonomous operations, logistics, command and control, and decision support. Effective use, however, depends not only on technical performance but also on how operators perceive, interpret, evaluate, and rely on AI outputs under uncertainty, time pressure, and adversarial interference. This study presents a conceptual integrative review informed by a structured supplementary literature search and synthesis. It synthesizes human factors, human–automation trust, human–AI teaming, military AI, and industrial engineering literature to develop an iterative multistage framework of human–AI trust in military applications. Trust is conceptualized as dynamic situational trust in a specific military AI system during task interaction, while dispositional, initial, and learned trust are treated as antecedent conditions. The framework distinguishes four analytically separable but functionally interdependent stages—perception, interpretation, evaluation, and trust judgment and reliance decision—and identifies four military-relevant moderators: system transparency, explainability, and behavioral predictability; data quality and information uncertainty; adversarial vulnerability; and operational and organizational context. The framework clarifies conceptual pathways to calibrated reliance, overtrust, and undertrust, and derives implications for task analysis, interface evaluation, human-centered design, operator training, and empirical validation.

items.title: Understanding tourist satisfaction in craft-based cultural tourism: a hybrid PLS-SEM, ANN and explainable AI approach
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze the linear structural relationships and nonlinear predictive contributions associated with tourist satisfaction in the Trusmi Batik Tourism Area. By integrating PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI, it evaluates how destination attributes function as hygiene or motivator factors. The ultimate goal is to develop a strategic quadrant matrix to guide local governments and destination managers in optimizing craft-based cultural tourism management. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a multi-stage hybrid design integrating PLS-SEM, an MLP-based artificial neural network (ANN) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) using SHAP analysis. PLS-SEM evaluates linear structural relationships based on the proposed theoretical hypotheses. A parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN captures complex, nonlinear predictive patterns. Finally, SHAP values interpret the model's hidden predictive contributions to construct an actionable strategic quadrant matrix. Findings The findings suggest that accessibility, resources, and the environment emerged as the primary “Star” motivators, with accessibility showing the strongest structural contribution and predictive importance among the examined constructs (ß = 0.310; |ϕ| = 0.416). “Batik Arts” emerged as the most influential indicator within the dataset. Services occupied the “Foundation” quadrant, whereas Facilities functioned primarily as a baseline hygiene factor and did not exhibit a statistically significant structural relationship with tourist satisfaction (ß = 0.014, p = 0.888). The parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN demonstrated promising predictive performance in capturing nonlinear patterns within this exploratory dataset. Research limitations/implications This study integrates PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI to examine linear and nonlinear patterns associated with tourist satisfaction within craft-based cultural tourism destinations. The findings suggest prioritizing immersive batik workshops, walkable heritage corridors, digital visitor information, and routine maintenance of basic facilities. The small, geographically focused sample limits generalizability and supports the need for external validation using larger and more diverse datasets. Practical implications This study offers a practical reference for tourism operators and local authorities to improve strategic resource allocation. Instead of funding costly luxury hotel expansions, managers could prioritize maintaining hygiene assets, including toilets, seating, and worship facilities. To enhance visitor satisfaction, investments may emphasize “Star” motivators through immersive batik-making workshops and authentic cultural experiences. Local governments may also improve urban micro-mobility by developing walkable sidewalks and flexible motorcycle routes throughout Trusmi's historic heritage corridors. These evidence-based recommendations support sustainable destination management while strengthening visitor experiences, cultural preservation, and long-term tourism resilience. Social implications This study has social implications for sustaining craft-based cultural tourism while strengthening community participation and cultural identity. The findings highlight the importance of accessible public spaces, immersive batik-making experiences, reliable visitor services, and heritage storytelling in supporting visitor engagement. Prioritizing these attributes can help local governments and tourism operators create more inclusive tourism environments that benefit visitors, artisans, and local communities. The framework also supports balanced resource allocation between basic hygiene facilities and culturally distinctive motivators. By strengthening artisan involvement, digital cultural communication, and heritage preservation, the approach can contribute to community resilience, intergenerational knowledge transmission, and sustainable tourism development. Originality/value The value of this study lies in its innovative hybrid framework integrating PLS-SEM, MLP-based ANN, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) within cultural tourism research. Compared with conventional linear approaches, the framework combines structural relationships, nonlinear predictive patterns, and SHAP-based interpretability to identify destination attributes with different levels of strategic importance.

items.title: Unethical Issues in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Among Undergraduates in Public Universities of Cross River State, Nigeria
items.abstract: The objective of the study is to investigate unethical issues in the use of Artificial intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public Universities in Cross River State. The study was conducted in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. Survey research design was adopted of the study. The population of this study comprised all final year students in the two public Universities in Cross River State. The population of final year students in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State comprised of 7,020 undergraduate students as recorded by Academic Planning Unit & Management Information System, 2023/2024 of the respective Universities. Stratified random sampling was adopted for the study. A total sample of 409 students which constitute 10% of the population of students in the study area sampling from population of 4081 students from fifty three (53) departments of University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. A questionnaire titled Unethical issues in the Use of Artificial intelligence Questionnaire (UIUAIQ) was developed by the researchers. This was subjected to face and content validity by three experts in measurement and evaluation in Faculty of Education University of Calabar. A trial tested on fifty (50) students from College of Health Technology Calabar to establish the reliability of the instrument. Cronbach Alpha coefficient was used to determine the reliability estimate of the instrument α = .70-.72. The instrument was administered to the respondents and retrieved with Zero attrition rate. This process was facilitated by the researcher and two trained research assistants. The data collected was analyzed through descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation. The findings of this study reveal a significant prevalence of unethical issues in the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public universities in Cross River State. Furthermore, the study also indicates a high level of overreliance on AI technologies among undergraduates, leading to reduced engagement in academic tasks and a decline in deep learning experiences. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that Higher institutions should incorporate AI ethics education into their curriculum to sensitize students about the ethical implications of AI misuse.

items.title: Using AI, Doubting AI: Developer Mental Models and Trust in AI-Assisted Software Work
items.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

items.title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Craft Patient-Facing Report Summaries: Opportunities for Enhancing Resident Training
items.abstract: IntroductionEffective patient communication is an essential skill for radiology and nuclear medicine specialists, yet it remains underemphasized in residency training. With increasing patient access to electronic medical records, the ability to translate technical reports into patient-facing summaries is critical. Generative AI may offer a dual benefit of improving workflow by producing patient-appropriate summaries and serving as a training tool to help residents hone their communication skills. MethodsSeventy-six de-identified nuclear medicine imaging procedure reports (covering general nuclear medicine, PET/CT (positron emission tomography-computed tomography), and nuclear cardiology) were used to generate 608 patient-facing summaries: four versions of each report were generated using ChatGPT models (o1-mini, 4o, 4o-mini, 4 legacy) and four versions were written by residents. Summaries adhered to a four-sentence maximum and targeted a sixth-grade reading level. GPT-4o was used to critique and rank AI-generated summaries, and the two best-performing AI versions were compared with resident summaries. Blinded evaluations by three experienced nuclear medicine physicians assessed summaries on readability, accuracy, appropriateness, and overall fitness for purpose. Likelihood Ratio Chi-Square tests assessed differences in performance. ResultsGPT o1-mini was ranked as the best summary in 86% of initial AI comparisons and 100% of final comparative assessments with resident summaries. GPT 4o and o1-mini outperformed residents across multiple domains including clarity, health literacy, and tone. The best human summaries were consistently outperformed by AI in both physician and AI assessments, though discrepancies in ranking priorities (e.g., tolerance for jargon vs. inaccuracy) were noted and AI more often produced summaries containing misinterpretations of data in the original reports. Resident summaries showed wide variation in tone, technicality, and patient appropriateness. Overall, 65% of all summaries (AI and human) were deemed fit-for-purpose. ConclusionGenerative AI models can produce consistently appropriate and readable patient-facing summaries of imaging procedure reports and may serve as effective tools to develop resident communication skills. Generative AI may therefore model best practices and provide timely feedback, offering structured opportunities to refine written communication. Future work should explore its integration into learner-tailored educational constructs using frameworks such as Bloom’s taxonomy, to enhance resident training and effectiveness of feedback mechanisms.

items.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education: Insights from ASLP students
items.abstract: Background Emerging artificial intelligence-based technologies are increasingly influencing teaching and learning practices in healthcare education, offering new opportunities for student engagement, learning, and skill development. Objective The purpose of this study was to explore utilization of artificial intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education based on insights from students. Further, to explore their awareness, use, perceived benefits, barriers, and attitudes toward the integration of artificial intelligence. Method A cross-sectional online survey of 17 questions was distributed to 483 audiology and speech-language pathology students enrolled in undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes across multiple institutions in India through social media platforms. The questionnaire was developed following a review of previously published studies examining students’ perceptions of the implications of artificial intelligence in education. Descriptive analysis was used to analyse the findings. Results A total of 286 students participated in the study (mean age = 21.73 ± 2.33 years), of whom 82.2% were females. Most participants (96.9%) were aware of artificial intelligence technologies, and 89.9% indicated using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. Regarding the future role of artificial intelligence in education, 75.1% disagreed that it could replace human lecturers. Students primarily used it for assignments and exam preparation, while limited institutional acceptance was a major barrier to its implementation. Conclusions Students expressed an optimistic view regarding the application of artificial intelligence in education. Students reported concerns about inaccurate artificial intelligence-generated information, while limited acceptance, inadequate knowledge, and ethical concerns hindered its effective integration into education.

items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.
